summary.text: 米 is a whole-graph picture of scattered grain. Its early referent was probably dehusked grain broadly; today it commonly means rice. The identity of the central stroke is disputed.

formation.text: Pictographic (象形): the marks around a central stroke depict scattered grain. The whole picture does not depend on identifying the central stroke, which has been interpreted as either a sieve or a grain stalk.

history.text: Early forms are described as small marks above and below a central stroke. The selected oracle-bone-style image is a modern redraw, not an ancient inscription. Forms are also listed for Chu manuscripts, bronze inscriptions, small seal script, and the Shuowen entry. One account says the dots were joined into strokes before the small-seal form, with Chu examples showing that this change had already begun. These descriptions do not establish a complete sequence of graphic changes.
The Shuowen entry explains 米 as grain seed and says the graph depicts the fruit of grain plants. This is an early dictionary interpretation of the graph’s form.

uncertainties.text: The central stroke has been interpreted as a sieve or a grain stalk; it may instead be a graphic separator. Its identity remains unresolved, but this does not affect the overall interpretation as a picture of grain.
The exact dates and contexts of reported early uses are unresolved, as is the chronology by which the broad grain sense came to be commonly rice-specific.

senses.text: The cited account reports oracle-bone use for rice or grain; scholarly discussion identifies the early referent as probably dehusked grain broadly, rather than one particular crop. The precise first-use date and inscription context are unresolved.
In common modern usage, 米 means rice.

In Japanese, 米 is used for the length unit metre after 米突 served as a sound-based rendering of French mètre. This is a separate borrowed word use, unrelated in meaning to grain. The exact route by which 米 alone became current is unresolved.

developments.text: The broad early grain sense is commonly specialized to rice in modern usage, though the chronology of this change is unresolved.

The written graph 米 was used for the unrelated word meaning ‘metre’ because 米突 provided a sound-based rendering of French mètre. This is a separate borrowing account, not a semantic development from ‘grain’; the date and route by which 米 alone became current are unresolved.

limitations.text: Other reported early uses include writing 敉 ‘pacify’, a sacrificial name, and clan names. Their inscription contexts and relationship, if any, to the grain meaning are unresolved, so they are not treated as semantic developments or separate senses.
Additional Japanese readings are listed, but their senses and histories are not explained here; the metre use is the one supported by the cited account.

overview.text: 米 pictures scattered grain. Its early meaning was probably dehusked grain broadly; today it commonly means rice. In Japanese, it also writes “metre”: 米突 rendered French mètre by sound, and 米 was later used as a shorter spelling.
